units.title: Brain Drain
units.intro: Grammar: the subject–verb–complement (SVC) pattern and clauses: noun phrases, noun clauses, adjective (relative) clauses and adjectival complements.

cards.title: SVC sentences and adjectival complements
rule: **SVC:** Subject + linking verb (*be, become, seem, look, feel*) + Complement (a noun or adjective that describes the subject): *Many graduates **became** doctors.* *The problem **seems** serious.*
An **adjectival complement** follows an adjective: *I am **happy to help**.* *She is **sure that she will return**.*

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: Since the local library was renovated last year, the number of visitors ________ significantly.

steps.text: The subject is 'the number of visitors' (singular).
The sentence describes an action that started in the past (renovated last year) and continues to have relevance in the present, requiring the present perfect tense ($$\text{has/have} + \text{V}_3$$).
Students often see 'visitors' (plural) and choose 'have increased' (Option B).

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: The science teacher asked Dawit, 'Why ________ your assignment on time yesterday?'

steps.text: This is a direct question in the past simple tense.
Option A incorrectly combines 'didn't' with the past tense verb 'completed'.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The rare African manuscript ________ from the national archives before the guards noticed the broken window.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The sentence describes two past events: the manuscript being stolen and the guards noticing the broken window. The theft happened before the guards noticed it, requiring the past perfect passive voice ($$\text{had been} + \text{V}_3$$).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Each of the candidates who applied for the engineering position ________ a written test.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The subject of the sentence is 'Each' (singular), which always takes a singular verb and auxiliary ($$\text{Each} \rightarrow \text{singular verb}$$).

cards.title: Adjective (relative) clauses
rule: An **adjective clause** describes a noun and begins with **who** (people), **which** (things), **that** (people or things), **whose** (possession), **where** (places), **when** (time): *Doctors **who leave the country** are hard to replace.*
**Defining** clauses tell us which one (no commas). **Non-defining** clauses add extra information (with commas; never *that*): *Asmara, **which is the capital**, is clean.*

examples.text: The engineer who designed the dam is Eritrean.
The book what I read was good.
examples.fix: The book that/which I read was good.

examples.text: My uncle, who lives abroad, sends money.

cards.title: Memory tip
body: **WHO** for people, **WHICH** for things, **WHERE** for places, **WHOSE** for owners.

cards.title: Unit summary
body: SVC sentences use a linking verb plus a complement (noun or adjective). Adjective clauses (who, which, that, whose, where, when) describe nouns; non-defining ones have commas and never use that. Adjectival complements complete adjectives (eager to, sure that).

glossary.meaning: A verb like be, seem, become that links the subject to a complement.
who, which, that, whose: starts an adjective clause.

tips.text: **WHO** for people, **WHICH** for things, **WHERE** for places, **WHOSE** for owners.
